It says that $K$ is geometrically normal over $k$: for every field extension $E/k$, $K\otimes_k E$ is normal. This uses separability in the finitely-generated-subextension sense stated in the hypothesis, not the narrower algebraic-separability class.

proof.text: The maps $K\otimes_k B\to B\otimes_k K$, $c\otimes b\mapsto b\otimes c$, and $B\otimes_k K\to K\otimes_k B$, $b\otimes c\mapsto c\otimes b$, respect additivity and the balancing relations $(cu)\otimes b=c\otimes(ub)$ for $u\in k$. Their composites fix pure tensors, so they are inverse maps. The tensor universal property and generation by pure tensors in [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] extend these balanced maps uniquely. The multiplication formula specified in the item shows they preserve products and the unit. This ring isomorphism sends prime ideals bijectively to prime ideals and induces isomorphisms of their localizations by $x/s\mapsto f(x)/f(s)$. Each localization on the target is therefore a domain; the induced fraction-field isomorphism carries monic equations and roots in both directions, so integral closedness is preserved. By [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], $B\otimes_k K$ is normal. For $B=0$ both tensor rings are zero and have no primes; disconnected $B$ is covered prime by prime.

title: Normal algebras remain normal under separable scalar extension
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $B$ be a commutative $k$-algebra, and let $K/k$ be a separable field extension [def-pc-field-extension, def-weil-pbc-separable-field-extension]: every finitely generated subextension is separably generated. Suppose $B$ is a normal ring [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], meaning that every prime localization of $B$ is an integrally closed domain. Then $B\otimes_k K$ is a normal ring: for every prime ideal $\mathfrak q$ of $B\otimes_k K$, the localization $(B\otimes_k K)_{\mathfrak q}$ is an integrally closed domain. Here the tensor product is the commutative tensor-product algebra [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], with $(b\otimes c)(b^{\prime}\otimes c^{\prime})=bb^{\prime}\otimes cc^{\prime}$ and unit $1\otimes1$. Neither algebraicity of $K/k$ nor finite generation of $B$ is required; the zero algebra and disconnected normal rings are included.
